subject: history
topicName: Nazi Racial Policy and the Holocaust

cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Racial Policy and the Holocaust
cards.back: The Nazis believed in a racial hierarchy with the "Aryan" race (tall, blonde, blue-eyed Germans and Nordics) at the top as the "master race" (Herrenvolk). At the bottom were "sub-humans" (Untermenschen) - Jews, Roma, Slavs, and black people. Hitler wrote in Mein Kampf (1925): "The Jew is and remains the eternal enemy of the Aryan."

cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Racial Policy and the Holocaust
cards.back: Persecution of Jews began immediately after Hitler became Chancellor. On 1 April 1933, the Nazis organised a nationwide boycott of Jewish shops and businesses. SA men stood outside Jewish shops with signs reading "Germans! Defend yourselves! Don't buy from Jews!"

cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Racial Policy and the Holocaust
cards.back: At the Nuremberg Rally on 15 September 1935, Hitler announced two laws that fundamentally changed the legal status of German Jews: the Reich Citizenship Law and the Law for the Protection of German Blood and Honour. These laws stripped Jews of citizenship and banned marriages between Jews and Germans.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Racial Policy and the Holocaust
cards.back: The Nuremberg Laws were a turning point because they made anti-Semitism legal and official. Before 1935, persecution had been through SA violence and local regulations; after 1935, it was enshrined in national law. This gave persecution the authority of the state and made it systematic.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Racial Policy and the Holocaust
cards.back: On the night of 9-10 November 1938, Nazi mobs attacked Jewish property across Germany in a organised pogrom called Kristallnacht ("Night of Broken Glass"). 191 synagogues were set on fire, over 7,000 Jewish shops were destroyed, 91 Jews were killed, and 20,000-30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Racial Policy and the Holocaust
cards.back: After Germany invaded Poland in September 1939, 2 million more Jews came under Nazi control. The Nazis forced Polish Jews into sealed, overcrowded areas called ghettos. The largest was the Warsaw Ghetto, where over 400,000 Jews were confined in an area of just 3.4 square km.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Racial Policy and the Holocaust
cards.back: On 20 January 1942, 15 senior Nazi officials met at a villa in Wannsee, a suburb of Berlin, to coordinate the "Final Solution to the Jewish Question." The conference was chaired by Reinhard Heydrich and organised by Adolf Eichmann. It formalised the systematic genocide of European Jews.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Racial Policy and the Holocaust
cards.back: The Final Solution (Endlösung) was the systematic, industrialised murder of European Jews. Six extermination camps were built in occupied Poland: Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec, Majdanek, and Chelmno. By the end of 1944, approximately 6 million Jews had been murdered.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Racial Policy and the Holocaust
cards.back: The death toll of the Holocaust was approximately 6 million Jews - two-thirds of all European Jews. Other victims of Nazi racial policy included 200,000-500,000 Roma (Gypsies), 200,000 disabled people (under the T4 "euthanasia" programme), and millions of Slavic civilians and Soviet prisoners of war.

cards.front: What should you know about history exam tips — nazi racial policy and the holocaust?
cards.back: 1. For Nazi Racial Policy and the Holocaust, include specific factual detail: dates, names, events and statistics where relevant 2. For source questions, analyse provenance (who, when, why, audience) before using the content 3. In evaluation questions, discuss multiple factors and weigh their relative significance 4. Always link back to the question focus — don't just narrate what happened with Nazi Racial Policy and the Holocaust 5. Use phrases like 'the most significant factor was... because...' to show analytical judgement
National boycott of Jewish shops (e.g. SA intimidation; many shops damaged; some Germans ignored the boycott)
Civil Service Law (e.g. Jews expelled from government jobs, teaching, and the judiciary)
Book burnings (e.g. Books by Jewish and "degenerate" authors burned publicly)
Law for Revocation of Citizenship (e.g. Naturalised Jews from Eastern Europe stripped of German citizenship)
Reich Chamber of Culture (e.g. Jews excluded from arts, music, literature, and journalism)
